title: Grade 10 Math Warm-Up
intro: Basic skills from middle school and freshman year, grouped by topic: an easy question to get the idea, then the same idea a step further. Take a hint if you need one; the worked solution comes after every answer.

questions.prompt: Which of these numbers is prime?
questions.hint: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. Try dividing each option by 3.
questions.why: 21 = 3 × 7, 27 = 3 × 9, and 33 = 3 × 11 all divide evenly by 3. 31 has no factors besides 1 and 31, so it is prime.
questions.no: Check whether each option divides evenly by 3.

questions.prompt: What is the prime factorization of 84?
questions.hint: Keep splitting until every factor is prime. 14 and 4 are not prime.
questions.why: Split it down: 84 = 4 × 21 = (2 × 2) × (3 × 7), which is 2² × 3 × 7. The other options stop early and leave a composite factor behind.
questions.no: Check whether every factor in your answer is actually prime.

questions.prompt: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 12 and 18?
questions.hint: List the factors of each number and find the biggest one they share.
questions.why: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. The largest they share is 6. Note that 36 is the least common multiple, not a factor.
questions.no: You're looking for the largest factor both numbers share.

questions.prompt: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 6 and 8?
questions.hint: Count up by 6s and by 8s until you hit the same number.
questions.why: Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24. Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. The first they share is 24. Multiplying them gives 48, which is a common multiple but not the least one.
questions.no: Multiplying the two numbers gives a common multiple, but not the smallest.

questions.prompt: What is 1/2 + 1/3?
questions.hint: You can't add fractions until the denominators match. Rewrite both over 6.
questions.why: 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6, so the sum is 5/6. Adding tops and bottoms straight across gives 2/5, which is the most common mistake here.
questions.no: Never add the denominators straight across.

questions.prompt: What is 2/3 ÷ 4/9?
questions.hint: Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal — flip the second one.
questions.why: Flip and multiply: 2/3 × 9/4 = 18/12, which reduces to 3/2, or 1½. Multiplying without flipping gives 8/27.
questions.no: Flip the second fraction, then multiply.

questions.prompt: What is 3.6 × 0.4?
questions.hint: Multiply as if there were no decimal points, then count the total decimal places.
questions.why: 36 × 4 = 144. There is 1 decimal place in 3.6 and 1 in 0.4, so 2 in total, giving 1.44.
questions.no: Count the decimal places in both numbers being multiplied.

questions.prompt: What is 0.144 ÷ 0.6?
questions.hint: Move the decimal point in both numbers until the one you're dividing by is a whole number.
questions.why: Multiply both by 10 to clear the divisor: 1.44 ÷ 6 = 0.24. Shifting both numbers the same amount leaves the answer unchanged.
questions.no: Shift both numbers by the same number of places first.

questions.prompt: Round 4.762 to the nearest tenth.
questions.hint: The tenths place is the first digit after the decimal point. Look at the digit just after it to decide.
questions.why: The tenths digit is 7, and the digit after it is 6, which is 5 or more, so round up to 4.8. Rounding to 4.76 stops at the hundredths place instead.
questions.no: Check which place value the tenths actually is.

questions.prompt: Without a calculator, which is the best estimate of 19.8 × 4.1?
questions.hint: Round each number to something easy first, then multiply.
questions.why: Round to 20 × 4 = 80. The exact answer is 81.18, so 80 is close. Estimating like this is the fastest way to rule out wrong multiple-choice answers on a timed test.
questions.no: Round each number to the nearest whole ten or one first.

questions.prompt: What is −8 + 3 × (−2)?
questions.hint: Multiply before you add, and watch the signs.
questions.why: Multiplication first: 3 × (−2) = −6. Then −8 + (−6) = −14.
questions.no: Do the multiplication before the addition.

questions.prompt: What is (−2)³ + (−4)(−3)?
questions.hint: An odd power of a negative stays negative. Two negatives multiplied give a positive.
questions.why: (−2)³ = −2 × −2 × −2 = −8, and (−4)(−3) = 12. So −8 + 12 = 4.
questions.no: Check the sign on the cube first.

questions.prompt: What is |−7|?
questions.hint: Absolute value is the distance from zero, and distance is never negative.
questions.why: −7 sits 7 units from zero on the number line, so its absolute value is 7. The bars strip the sign; they don't double the number.
questions.no: Absolute value asks how far from zero, ignoring direction.

questions.prompt: What is |3 − 10| + |−2|?
questions.hint: Work out what's inside each set of bars first, then take the absolute value of each.
questions.why: Inside the first bars: 3 − 10 = −7, so |−7| = 7. The second gives |−2| = 2. Then 7 + 2 = 9. Simplify inside the bars before stripping the sign.
questions.no: Simplify inside the bars first, then take absolute values.

questions.prompt: What is 5 + 2 × 3?
questions.hint: Multiplication comes before addition, no matter which is written first.
questions.why: Multiply first: 2 × 3 = 6, then 5 + 6 = 11. Working strictly left to right gives 21, which is the trap.
questions.no: Left to right isn't the rule — multiplication comes first.

questions.prompt: What is (8 − 3)² ÷ 5 + 4?
questions.hint: Parentheses, then the exponent, then divide, then add.
questions.why: Parentheses: 8 − 3 = 5. Exponent: 5² = 25. Divide: 25 ÷ 5 = 5. Add: 5 + 4 = 9. Adding before dividing would give 29.
questions.no: Finish the division before you add.

questions.prompt: What is 3⁴?
questions.hint: That's four 3s multiplied together, not 3 times 4.
questions.why: 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81. Multiplying the base by the exponent gives 12, which is the classic misread.
questions.no: An exponent means repeated multiplication, not multiplying base by exponent.

questions.prompt: Simplify: x³ · x⁵
questions.hint: Write it out as x's multiplied together and count them.
questions.why: Three x's times five x's is eight x's: x⁸. When multiplying powers of the same base you add the exponents; multiplying them gives x¹⁵, which is a different rule entirely.
questions.no: Add the exponents when multiplying like bases.

questions.prompt: What is √144?
questions.hint: What number, multiplied by itself, gives 144?
questions.why: 12 × 12 = 144, so √144 = 12. Halving 144 gives 72, which is a different operation entirely.
questions.no: Try squaring each option to test it.

questions.prompt: Which of these is √50 in simplest radical form?
questions.hint: Look for the largest perfect square that divides 50.
questions.why: 50 = 25 × 2, and 25 is a perfect square, so √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2. Check it: 5√2 ≈ 7.07, and 7.07² ≈ 50. ✓
questions.no: Pull out the perfect square factor.

questions.prompt: Write 4.5 × 10³ in standard form.
questions.hint: The exponent tells you how many places to move the decimal point to the right.
questions.why: Moving the decimal 3 places right turns 4.5 into 4,500. Equivalently, 4.5 × 1000 = 4500.
questions.no: Count the decimal places you moved.

questions.prompt: Write 0.00072 in scientific notation.
questions.hint: Move the decimal until exactly one non-zero digit sits in front of it, then count the moves. Small numbers take a negative exponent.
questions.why: Moving the decimal 4 places right gives 7.2, so the exponent is −4. The 72 version has two digits before the decimal, which isn't proper scientific notation.
questions.no: Exactly one non-zero digit belongs in front of the decimal.

questions.prompt: What comes next in the pattern? 2, 6, 18, 54, ___
questions.hint: Look at what each term is multiplied by, not what's added.
questions.why: Each term is multiplied by 3: 2 → 6 → 18 → 54, so the next is 54 × 3 = 162.
questions.no: Check for multiplication rather than addition.

questions.prompt: What comes next in the pattern? 3, 7, 15, 31, ___
questions.hint: The gaps between terms are 4, 8, 16. What comes next in that list?
questions.why: The differences double each time: 4, 8, 16, then 32. So 31 + 32 = 63. Another way to see it: each term is double the one before, plus 1.
questions.no: Look at the differences between terms, then at how those differences change.

questions.prompt: A jacket normally costs $48. It is on sale for 25% off. What is the sale price?
questions.hint: 25% off means you still pay 75% of the original price.
questions.why: 25% of $48 is $12, so the sale price is 48 − 12 = $36. Shortcut: 0.75 × 48 = 36.
questions.no: The discount isn't the answer — subtract it from the original.

questions.prompt: After a 20% discount, a pair of shoes costs $36. What was the original price?
questions.hint: $36 represents 80% of the original, not 100%. Work backwards.
questions.why: If the price dropped 20%, then $36 is 80% of the original: 0.80x = 36, so x = 36 ÷ 0.8 = $45. Adding 20% back onto $36 gives $43.20, which is the classic trap — percentages are taken from different starting numbers.
questions.no: Adding 20% back on doesn't undo a 20% discount.

questions.prompt: A car travels 150 miles on 6 gallons of gas. At the same rate, how far can it travel on 10 gallons?
questions.hint: Find the miles per gallon first.
questions.why: 150 ÷ 6 = 25 miles per gallon, and 25 × 10 = 250 miles.
questions.no: Try finding the unit rate first.

questions.prompt: If 3 painters can paint a room in 8 hours, how long would 4 painters take working at the same rate?
questions.hint: More painters means less time. This one runs the opposite way to the usual proportion.
questions.why: The job takes 3 × 8 = 24 painter-hours in total. With 4 painters that's 24 ÷ 4 = 6 hours. Watch for this reversal: adding workers shrinks the time rather than growing it.
questions.no: Should more painters take more time or less?

questions.prompt: How many inches are in 4 feet?
questions.hint: There are 12 inches in a foot.
questions.why: 4 × 12 = 48 inches. Going from a larger unit to a smaller one always multiplies, so the number gets bigger.
questions.no: Multiply by 12 when converting feet to inches.

questions.prompt: A car travels at 60 miles per hour. How far does it travel in 20 minutes?
questions.hint: 20 minutes is a third of an hour. The rate is given per hour.
questions.why: 20 minutes is 20/60 = ⅓ of an hour, so the car covers 60 × ⅓ = 20 miles. Multiplying 60 by 20 without converting the minutes gives 1,200, and dividing carelessly gives 3.
questions.no: Convert the minutes to a fraction of an hour first.

questions.prompt: Simplify: 4(x + 3) − 2x
questions.hint: Distribute the 4 across both terms, then combine like terms.
questions.why: Distributing gives 4x + 12 − 2x. Combining the x terms: 4x − 2x = 2x, leaving 2x + 12.
questions.no: The 4 multiplies both the x and the 3.

questions.prompt: Evaluate 2a² − 3b when a = −3 and b = 4.
questions.hint: Square the −3 before multiplying by 2. The square makes it positive.
questions.why: a² = (−3)² = 9, so 2a² = 18. Then 3b = 12, and 18 − 12 = 6. Squaring before multiplying is what keeps this positive.
questions.no: Apply the exponent before the multiplication.

questions.prompt: Solve for x: 3x − 7 = 20
questions.hint: Undo the subtraction before you undo the multiplication.
questions.why: Add 7 to both sides for 3x = 27, then divide by 3 to get x = 9. Check: 3(9) − 7 = 20. ✓
questions.no: Watch the order you undo the operations.

questions.prompt: Solve for x: 5x − 3 = 2x + 12
questions.hint: Get all the x terms onto one side first.
questions.why: Subtract 2x from both sides: 3x − 3 = 12. Add 3: 3x = 15, so x = 5. Check: 5(5) − 3 = 22 and 2(5) + 12 = 22. ✓
questions.no: Collect the x terms on one side before solving.

questions.prompt: Solve: x + 5 > 12
questions.hint: Solve it exactly like an equation — subtract 5 from both sides.
questions.why: Subtracting 5 from both sides gives x > 7. Adding and subtracting work the same as with an equals sign; the inequality symbol doesn't change.
questions.no: Subtract 5 from both sides, as you would with an equation.

questions.prompt: Solve: −3x > 12
questions.hint: When you divide both sides by a negative number, the inequality symbol flips direction.
questions.why: Divide both sides by −3 to get x < −4 — the symbol flips because you divided by a negative. Test it: x = −5 gives −3(−5) = 15, which is greater than 12. ✓
questions.no: Dividing by a negative flips the inequality.

questions.prompt: What are the solutions to x² − 9 = 0?
questions.hint: What numbers, when squared, give 9?
questions.why: x² = 9, and both 3² = 9 and (−3)² = 9. A quadratic like this has two solutions, so leaving off the negative loses half the answer.
questions.no: Don't forget the negative root.

questions.prompt: What are the solutions to x² + 5x − 24 = 0?
questions.hint: Find two numbers that multiply to −24 and add to 5.
questions.why: 8 × (−3) = −24 and 8 + (−3) = 5, so it factors as (x + 8)(x − 3) = 0, giving x = −8 and x = 3. Note the signs flip from the factors to the solutions.
questions.no: Check the signs — the factors and the solutions have opposite ones.

questions.prompt: A town's population is 2,400 and grows by 5% in one year. What is the population after that year?
questions.hint: Find 5% of 2,400, then add it on. Or multiply by 1.05 in one step.
questions.why: 5% of 2,400 is 120, so the population becomes 2400 + 120 = 2520. In one step: 2400 × 1.05 = 2520.

questions.prompt: That same town of 2,400 people grows by 5% every year. What is the population after 2 years?
questions.hint: The second year's 5% is calculated on the new, larger population.
questions.why: Year 1: 2400 × 1.05 = 2520. Year 2: 2520 × 1.05 = 2646. Growth compounds, so it beats the 2,640 you'd get by adding 5% of the original twice.
questions.no: The second year grows from 2,520, not from 2,400.

questions.prompt: Two lines that cross at a right angle are called:
questions.hint: Think of the corner of a square, or a plus sign.
questions.why: Perpendicular lines meet at 90°. Parallel lines never meet at all. Congruent means identical in size and shape, and similar means same shape at a different size — both describe figures, not the angle between lines.
questions.no: Parallel lines never cross at all.

questions.prompt: A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides is called a:
questions.hint: The other three shapes listed all have two pairs of parallel sides.
questions.why: A trapezoid has exactly one pair of parallel sides. A parallelogram, rhombus, and rectangle each have two pairs, which is what separates them from a trapezoid.
questions.no: Count how many pairs of parallel sides each shape has.

questions.prompt: Two angles are complementary. One measures 35°. What does the other measure?
questions.hint: Complementary angles add to 90°. Supplementary angles add to 180° — don't mix them up.
questions.why: 90 − 35 = 55°. If they had been supplementary, adding to 180°, the answer would be 145°, which is why the two words are worth keeping straight.
questions.no: Complementary means adding to 90°, not 180°.

questions.prompt: Two angles are supplementary, and one is three times the size of the other. What is the smaller angle?
questions.hint: Call the smaller angle x. Then the larger is 3x, and together they make 180°.
questions.why: x + 3x = 180, so 4x = 180 and x = 45°. The larger angle is 135°, and the two do add to 180°. ✓
questions.no: Write both angles in terms of one variable first.

questions.prompt: A square has an area of 81 square inches. What is its perimeter?
questions.hint: Find the side length first — what number times itself is 81?
questions.why: Since 9 × 9 = 81, each side is 9 inches, and the perimeter is 4 × 9 = 36 inches.
questions.no: Find the side length before the perimeter.

questions.prompt: A rectangle has a length of 12 cm and a perimeter of 34 cm. What is its area?
questions.hint: Use the perimeter to find the missing width first.
questions.why: P = 2l + 2w, so 34 = 24 + 2w and the width is 5 cm. Area is 12 × 5 = 60 cm². This runs the reverse of the square problem: perimeter in, area out.
questions.no: Solve for the width using the perimeter formula.

questions.prompt: A circle has a diameter of 10 cm. What is its circumference? (Use π ≈ 3.14)
questions.hint: Circumference is π × diameter. You're given the diameter already.
questions.why: C = πd = 3.14 × 10 = 31.4 cm. Using the radius by mistake gives 15.7, and using the area formula gives 78.5.
questions.no: Circumference uses the diameter; area uses the radius squared.

questions.prompt: A circle has a diameter of 12 inches. What is its area, in terms of π?
questions.hint: The area formula needs the radius, but you've been handed the diameter. Halve it first.
questions.why: The radius is 12 ÷ 2 = 6. Then A = πr² = π(6²) = 36π square inches. Squaring the diameter instead gives 144π, the usual slip.
questions.no: Convert diameter to radius before squaring.

questions.prompt: What is the volume of a rectangular box measuring 3 cm by 4 cm by 5 cm?
questions.hint: Volume of a box is length times width times height.
questions.why: 3 × 4 × 5 = 60 cm³. The answer 94 is the surface area of the same box, which is a different question.
questions.no: Multiply all three dimensions together.

questions.prompt: What is the total surface area of a cube with edges of 4 inches?
questions.hint: A cube has 6 identical square faces. Find the area of one, then account for all of them.
questions.why: Each face is 4 × 4 = 16 in², and a cube has 6 faces, so 6 × 16 = 96 in². The answer 64 is the cube's volume, not its surface area.
questions.no: Find one face's area, then multiply by 6.

questions.prompt: Two triangles are congruent. What does that tell you about them?
options: They have the same perimeter but may differ in shape
questions.hint: Congruent and similar are different words. One allows resizing, the other doesn't.
questions.why: Congruent figures are identical: matching side lengths and matching angles. Similar figures have the same shape at a different scale. Congruent triangles are always similar, but similar triangles are only congruent when the scale factor is 1.
questions.no: That describes similar triangles, not congruent ones.

questions.prompt: Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF. Side AB measures 7 cm, and angle A measures 40°. What can you conclude?
questions.hint: The letter order tells you which parts match up: A pairs with D, B with E, C with F.
questions.why: In congruent triangles, corresponding parts are equal. The naming order pairs A with D and B with E, so AB corresponds to DE and measures 7 cm, and angle D matches angle A at 40°.
questions.no: Congruent means the matching parts are equal, not scaled.

questions.prompt: Triangle A has sides 4, 6, and 8. Triangle B is similar to Triangle A, and its shortest side is 10. What is Triangle B's longest side?
questions.hint: Find the scale factor from the shortest sides, then apply it to the longest.
questions.why: The scale factor is 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5. Triangle A's longest side is 8, so Triangle B's longest is 8 × 2.5 = 20.
questions.no: Match corresponding sides before scaling.

questions.prompt: A 6-foot-tall person casts a 4-foot shadow. At the same time, a nearby tree casts a 22-foot shadow. How tall is the tree?
questions.hint: The person and the tree form similar triangles with their shadows. Set up matching ratios.
questions.why: Height over shadow is the same for both: 6/4 = h/22. Cross-multiplying gives 4h = 132, so h = 33 feet. The trap is subtracting or adding instead of scaling.
questions.no: Keep height over shadow on both sides of the proportion.

questions.prompt: A 13-foot ladder leans against a wall with its base 5 feet from the wall. How high up the wall does the ladder reach?
questions.hint: The ladder is the hypotenuse, not a leg.
questions.why: By the Pythagorean theorem, 5² + h² = 13², so h² = 144 and h = 12 feet. This is the familiar 5-12-13 right triangle.
questions.no: The 13 is the longest side, so it's the hypotenuse.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has a hypotenuse of 10 and one leg of 6. What is its area?
questions.hint: You need both legs before you can find the area. Find the missing one first.
questions.why: The missing leg: 6² + b² = 10² gives b² = 64 and b = 8. Area of a triangle is ½ × 6 × 8 = 24. Using the hypotenuse as a base gives 30, which is the trap here.
questions.no: The two legs form the right angle — the hypotenuse isn't one of them.

questions.prompt: In which quadrant does the point (−3, 5) lie?
questions.hint: Quadrants are numbered counterclockwise starting from the top right. A negative x means left of the y-axis.
questions.why: A negative x puts the point left of center, and a positive y puts it above center: the upper-left region, which is Quadrant II.
questions.no: Negative x means left; positive y means up.

questions.prompt: What is the distance between the points (2, 3) and (2, 9)?
questions.hint: Both points share the same x value, so this is a straight vertical line. No formula needed.
questions.why: Since the x values match, the points sit on a vertical line and the distance is just the gap in y: 9 − 3 = 6. Adding the coordinates instead gives 12.
questions.no: Same x means a vertical line — just subtract the y values.

questions.prompt: What is the slope of the line through the points (1, 2) and (5, 10)?
questions.hint: Slope is rise over run: the change in y divided by the change in x.
questions.why: (10 − 2) ÷ (5 − 1) = 8 ÷ 4 = 2. Flipping the fraction gives ½, a common slip.
questions.no: Divide the change in y by the change in x, in that order.

questions.prompt: What is the equation of the line passing through the points (−2, 3) and (4, 15)?
questions.hint: Find the slope, then substitute one point to solve for the y-intercept.
questions.why: Slope = (15 − 3) ÷ (4 − (−2)) = 12 ÷ 6 = 2. Substituting (4, 15) into y = 2x + b gives 15 = 8 + b, so b = 7.
questions.no: The slope is right in two options — check the intercept.

questions.prompt: A line on a graph passes through (0, 2) and (3, 8). Following the same trend, what value of y would you expect at x = 5?
questions.hint: Work out how much y climbs for each single step in x, then extend it.
questions.why: y rises 6 while x rises 3, a rate of 2 per unit. From x = 3 to x = 5 is 2 more units, so y climbs another 4: 8 + 4 = 12.
questions.no: Find the rate of change between the given points first.

questions.prompt: A graph plots a car's total distance travelled against time. Between hour 2 and hour 3, the line is completely flat. What does that mean?
options: The car kept a steady speed
questions.hint: On a distance-time graph, the steepness of the line is the speed.
questions.why: A flat line means the total distance didn't change during that hour, so the car covered no ground: it was stopped. A steady speed would show as a straight line sloping upward, not a flat one.
questions.ok: Read the shape, not just the numbers.
questions.no: Ask what a flat line says about the distance changing.

questions.prompt: What is the mode of this set? 3, 5, 5, 8, 9, 5, 2
questions.hint: The mode is the value that shows up most often. Just count.
questions.why: 5 appears three times; every other value appears once. The mode is 5. Note that 5.3 is roughly the mean, which is a different measure entirely.
questions.no: The mode is about frequency, not size or average.

questions.prompt: What is the median of this set? 4, 8, 11, 15
questions.hint: With an even count there's no single middle value. Average the two in the middle.
questions.why: Ordered, the two middle values are 8 and 11. Their average is (8 + 11) ÷ 2 = 9.5. With an odd count you'd just pick the middle number, but an even count needs this extra step.
questions.no: With an even count, average the two middle values.

questions.prompt: A student's five test scores are 70, 78, 85, 85, and 92. What is the mean score?
questions.hint: Add all five, then divide by 5. Note that 85 is the median and the mode — a common trap.
questions.why: The scores total 410, and 410 ÷ 5 = 82. The median and mode are both 85, so the mean is the odd one out here.
questions.no: That's a different measure of center.

questions.prompt: A student has averaged 82 across four tests. What score is needed on the fifth test to bring the average up to 85?
questions.hint: Work with totals rather than averages: what must all five scores add up to?
questions.why: Four tests at an 82 average total 4 × 82 = 328. Five tests averaging 85 must total 5 × 85 = 425. The difference is 425 − 328 = 97. Pulling an average up takes more than the target itself.
questions.no: Convert both averages into totals first.

questions.prompt: A bag holds 4 red marbles, 5 blue marbles, and 3 green marbles. If one marble is drawn at random, what is the probability that it is NOT blue?
questions.hint: How many marbles are there in total, and how many of them are not blue?
questions.why: There are 12 marbles in all, and 4 + 3 = 7 are not blue, giving 7/12. You could also compute 1 − 5/12.
questions.no: Count the total marbles again.

questions.prompt: From that same bag of 4 red, 5 blue, and 3 green marbles, two marbles are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
questions.hint: After the first red is drawn, both the reds and the total are one smaller.
questions.why: First draw: 4/12. Second draw: only 3 reds remain out of 11 marbles, so 3/11. Multiply: 4/12 × 3/11 = 12/132 = 1/11. If the marble were put back, you'd get 1/9 instead.
questions.no: The second draw comes from a smaller bag.
